strengths: Addresses a well-motivated gap: unifying spatial, functional, and part-level (affordance) 3D scene graphs into a single representation, which is clearly demonstrated to be missing from prior spatial-only or functional-only 3DSG work via a clear motivating figure (Fig. 2) showing failure of CLIP/GroundingDINO on part-level prompts.

The system design is coherent and each component is well-motivated: knowledge-guided entity-space control to compensate for part-detection failures, color-distribution features for part association (since parts tend to be single-material, unlike objects), and a geometry-initialized prior graph with verification-gated multi-agent LLM reasoning to avoid the quadratic blow-up of naive pairwise relation inference.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation: node/edge/affordance recall, node localization sensitivity (IoU/IoP), and thorough ablations isolating the contribution of each proposed component (knowledge base, color feature, prior graph, split-LLM design), all showing consistent and often large improvements over strengthened baselines (including with GPT-5 backbones for fairness).

The new UniGraph3D benchmark consolidates and substantially extends existing functional 3DSG datasets (FunGraph3D, SceneFun3D) with unified annotation of object-part hierarchy, spatial and functional relations, and affordances, addressing a genuine lack of an evaluation resource for the unified-3DSG task and enabling more consistent comparison across method families that were previously evaluated in isolation.

Demonstrated applicability beyond benchmark numbers: real robot deployment (Stretch3) for QA, task planning, and language-conditioned navigation illustrates practical value of the unified graph representation, going beyond a purely academic contribution.
weaknesses: The benchmark (UniGraph3D) is built by the same authors proposing the method, and details of the annotation process, inter-annotator agreement, and scale (only 251 object nodes / 414 part nodes total, fairly small) are relegated to supplementary material; this raises reproducibility and independent-verification concerns for a benchmark contribution meant to be a standard evaluation resource.

Node localization is evaluated only at a very loose non-zero IoU threshold in the main tables; the stricter analysis in Table 4 reveals OP3DSG's part-node localization is actually mediocre (IoU≥0.10: 25.8 vs. KeySG's 30.4; IoP≥0.25: 13.0 vs. KeySG's 23.4), indicating that much of the headline part-node gain in Table 2 may be driven by retrieval/labeling improvements rather than genuinely better 3D localization of small parts — this caveat is somewhat underplayed in the text.

The object-part knowledge base K is described as 'empirically curated' without details on its size, coverage, construction methodology, or how the method would generalize to object categories/part types outside this curated base; this limits the claimed 'open-vocabulary' generality of the part-detection stage, since the ablation (w/o knowledge) shows performance collapses substantially without it.

The comparison baselines (ConceptGraph, OpenFunGraph, FunGraph) are not originally designed for the unified-graph task and had to be reimplemented/extended by the authors with additional LLM prompting; while reasonable, this introduces potential bias in how fairly these baselines are tuned/extended relative to the proposed method, and no ablation of alternative baseline-extension strategies is given.

Several method components (greedy online association, thresholds for edge-candidate neighborhoods at 1 meter, similarity aggregation weights) rely on hand-set hyperparameters without sensitivity analysis, raising questions about robustness across differently scaled/furnished scenes.

Efficiency/runtime and scalability of the multi-agent LLM reasoning pipeline (cost, latency, comparison with baselines) are not reported quantitatively, despite the paper's repeated claims of avoiding scalability bottlenecks compared to VLM-based captioning approaches.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine gap in the literature: existing 3DSG approaches split into object-centric spatial graphs and function-centric graphs with limited part-level grounding, and the motivating preliminary experiments (Fig. 2, CLIP/GroundingDINO failing on part-level prompts) make a convincing case for the problem.

The proposed pipeline is reasonably well engineered, combining knowledge-guided part-candidate expansion, geometry+semantic+color-histogram based multi-view fusion for small parts, and a decomposed multi-agent LLM reasoning scheme (local/remote/affordance) anchored on a geometry-initialized prior graph to control the combinatorial explosion of relation inference.

Extensive ablations (Table 5) isolate the contribution of each component (knowledge base, color-distribution features, prior graph, split-LLM design), and the results consistently support the design choices.

The UniGraph3D benchmark consolidates and re-annotates two prior functional-3DSG datasets with object-part spatial relations and affordances, filling an evaluation gap since prior benchmarks evaluated spatial and functional aspects in isolation.

Reasonably comprehensive quantitative comparisons against multiple recent baselines (ConceptGraph, FunGraph, OpenFunGraph, KeySG), including both original and GPT-5-upgraded variants, and qualitative + real-robot demonstrations illustrating downstream applicability (QA, task planning, navigation).
weaknesses: The claimed 'open-vocabulary' capability is substantially undermined by the reliance on a hand-curated object-part knowledge base (Sec. 4.2) and a lexical containment heuristic (object label contained in part label string) for building the prior graph; the system's ability to handle genuinely novel object-part combinations not anticipated by this manually built knowledge base is untested and likely fragile, contradicting the open-vocabulary framing emphasized throughout the paper.

UniGraph3D is quite small in absolute scale (251 object nodes, 414 part nodes, 425 functional/spatial edges total across the whole benchmark per Table 1), raising concerns about statistical robustness of the reported gains and about whether the benchmark can meaningfully evaluate generalization versus overfitting to a narrow set of object/part categories seen during knowledge-base curation.

Despite large gains in node/edge retrieval metrics, the stricter localization analysis (Table 4) shows OP3DSG's part-node localization remains weak (e.g., IoU≥0.10: 25.8, IoP≥0.25: 13.0), and is actually worse than KeySG on IoP, suggesting the headline retrieval-based improvements may partly reflect the CLIP-similarity top-K matching protocol rather than genuinely precise part-level 3D grounding.

The paper relies heavily on closed-source, non-reproducible LLMs (GPT-4/GPT-5 via API) for the core relation/affordance reasoning stage, which raises reproducibility concerns and makes the reported numbers dependent on proprietary model versions that may change or become inaccessible.

No computational cost/runtime analysis is provided for the multi-stage pipeline (multiple detector passes, multi-view fusion, multiple parallel LLM agent calls per scene), which is important given the paper's claims about scalability and its proposed use as a real-time perception backbone for embodied robots.

The real-world robot demonstrations (Sec. 6) are purely qualitative/illustrative (figure + demo video) with no quantitative success rates, failure analysis, or comparison against baselines on the actual robot tasks, weakening the claimed impact on 'diverse real-world robotics tasks.'

Baseline extensions (adding part/functional/spatial reasoning to ConceptGraph and OpenFunGraph via 'the same prompting strategy') are done by the authors rather than being the baselines' original designs, and details of this adaptation are not given in the main text, leaving some ambiguity about whether the comparison is fully fair to the strongest possible baseline configurations.

There is little discussion of failure modes or hallucination rates of the LLM-based verification-gated reasoning, despite this being framed as a key mechanism to 'avoid hallucinations' — an empirical hallucination/error-rate analysis would substantially strengthen this claim.

strengths: The paper identifies a well-motivated gap: existing open-vocabulary 3DSGs are largely object-centric and either lack fine-grained part-level nodes or lack unified spatial+functional+affordance representation. The motivating preliminary experiments (Fig. 2) showing CLIP/GroundingDINO failure modes on part-centric prompts are a nice, concrete justification for the technical approach.

The proposed pipeline is a coherent systems-level integration: knowledge-guided object-part candidate expansion, part-aware multi-view fusion using both semantic and color-distribution cues, and a decomposed multi-agent LLM reasoning scheme with geometry-anchored verification. Each design choice is tied to a specific failure mode (part omission, part-association instability, relation hallucination/scalability), and the ablation study (Table 5) supports that each component contributes meaningfully.

The new UniGraph3D benchmark is a genuine and useful contribution: it consolidates and re-annotates two prior functional-3DSG datasets with additional spatial relations and expanded affordance labels, addressing an important gap since no prior benchmark jointly tests part-aware perception and multi-level relational reasoning (Table 1).

Extensive quantitative comparison against reasonably strong and updated baselines (ConceptGraph, FunGraph, OpenFunGraph, KeySG), with both original and GPT-5-upgraded variants, strengthens the claim that gains come from the proposed architecture rather than merely a stronger LLM backbone.

Real-world robot demonstrations (question answering, task planning, navigation) on a physical platform (Stretch3) add practical validation beyond static benchmark numbers, supporting the applied/systems relevance of the contribution.
weaknesses: The knowledge base K for object-part candidate generation is described as 'empirically curated' with no details on size, coverage, construction methodology, or how it generalizes to truly novel objects outside the curated set — this could undermine the open-vocabulary claim if the part vocabulary is effectively closed-set via the KB, and the ablation shows this component is the single largest contributor to performance (Table 5), making its opacity a significant reproducibility concern.

The node localization sensitivity study (Table 4) shows OP3DSG's part-node IoU/IoP scores (25.8/13.0) are notably lower than KeySG (30.4/23.4), indicating that despite superior semantic retrieval, geometric localization of small parts remains a real limitation understated in the main narrative, which emphasizes overall gains.

The LLM-based relation/affordance reasoning modules are only described at a high level (three parallel agents, chain-of-thought prompting, verification gate); the actual prompts, error/hallucination rates, and failure analysis (e.g., cases where the KB-based lexical heuristic for part-object matching fails, such as ambiguous names not literally containing the object string) are not shown, limiting insight into robustness and reproducibility.

UniGraph3D, while a useful contribution, is built by augmenting only two existing indoor datasets (FunGraph3D and SceneFun3D) with modest total statistics (251 objects, 414 parts across the whole benchmark), which may limit diversity and statistical significance of the reported comparisons relative to larger-scale scene graph benchmarks.

The paper does not report computational cost/runtime comparisons (e.g., wall-clock graph construction time, LLM API calls/cost) despite explicitly motivating the design around 'scalability' and avoiding VLM captioning overhead — a quantitative efficiency comparison against OpenFunGraph's captioning-based approach would substantiate this central claimed advantage.

Only a single qualitative figure (partial 3DSG in two scenes) is provided; no failure-case qualitative analysis is shown, which would help readers understand the limits of the part-detection and reasoning pipeline in more cluttered or ambiguous real-world scenes.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: the paper convincingly identifies a real gap (spatial vs. functional 3DSGs are treated separately, and open-vocabulary part-level grounding fails with off-the-shelf CLIP/GroundingDINO), backed by a clear preliminary experiment (Fig. 2).

The proposed Unified 3D Scene Graph formulation (objects, parts, spatial/functional relations, affordances in one graph) is a sensible and useful abstraction for embodied tasks, and the technical pipeline (knowledge-guided part candidate expansion, part-aware color-distribution fusion, geometry-initialized prior graph + multi-agent verification-gated LLM reasoning) is coherent and specifically designed to address the stated challenges (small/ambiguous parts, quadratic relation search space, LLM hallucination).

Comprehensive experimental validation: node/edge recall, affordance recall, node localization sensitivity (IoU/IoP), thorough ablations isolating each component's contribution, efficiency analysis (GPU memory, VLM/LLM call counts) showing large efficiency gains over VLM-captioning baselines, and generalization checks on a purely object-centric benchmark (ReplicaSSG) and per-source-dataset evaluation.

Introduces UniGraph3D, a consolidated and re-annotated benchmark unifying FunGraph3D and SceneFun3D with explicit object-part spatial relations and affordance annotations, addressing labeling inconsistencies in prior datasets (detailed in supplementary with relation-label refinement and affordance taxonomy).

Demonstrates practical downstream utility with real-world robot deployment across multiple embodied tasks (QA, task planning, language-conditioned navigation), going beyond offline benchmark numbers to show the graph is actionable.
Honest discussion of failure cases (fragmented towel bar, reflected object misdetected, remote-control confusions) rather than hiding limitations.
weaknesses: Core novelty is largely in system integration/engineering (combining existing open-vocab detectors RAM/VLPart/SAM, classical color-distribution features, and LLM agents) rather than a new learned model or theoretical insight; this should be judged as an applied/systems contribution, which the paper does not explicitly flag as such.

The main baselines (ConceptGraph, OpenFunGraph) are extended by the authors themselves with added part/relation-inference prompting to make them comparable; since the authors design these extensions, there is some risk that the comparison is not fully calibrated to the baselines' best possible configurations, which could bias the reported margins.

Node/edge retrieval metrics rely on soft top-K matching via CLIP/Sentence-BERT embedding similarity, which can be lenient and may not fully capture localization/labeling precision; Table 4 shows part-node localization remains weak under strict IoU/IoP thresholds, a meaningful limitation not fully resolved by the method.

The affordance space is restricted to 9 fixed categories (adopted from prior work), which is not truly open-vocabulary and could limit generality of affordance predictions in more diverse real-world settings.

The intra-object edge pruning relies on a lexical heuristic (part label text containment in object label), which is somewhat brittle and may not generalize to object-part naming conventions outside the curated knowledge base.
Real-world robot demonstrations (Sec. 6) are presented qualitatively via a demo video/figure without quantitative success-rate metrics, limiting the strength of the claimed real-world impact.

Benchmark scale/diversity (a few hundred scenes/objects consolidated from two existing small datasets) is modest, and annotation quality assurance (e.g., inter-annotator agreement) is not reported, which affects confidence in the benchmark as a long-term community resource.

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation: the paper clearly identifies a gap (existing 3DSGs are either object-centric spatial graphs or function-centric graphs, but not both) and supports this with a targeted preliminary experiment (Fig. 2) showing CLIP and GroundingDINO fail to ground part-level phrases distinctly from object-level ones.

The proposed 'Unified 3D Scene Graph' task and the OP3DSG pipeline (knowledge-guided part candidate generation, part-aware multi-view fusion with color-distribution cues, and a geometry-anchored/verification-gated multi-agent LLM reasoning stage) is a coherent, well-engineered system with clear technical descriptions and equations for each stage.

A new benchmark, UniGraph3D, is constructed by consolidating and substantially re-annotating two existing datasets (FunGraph3D, SceneFun3D), including careful relation-label de-duplication/canonicalization and new spatial/affordance annotations — a useful resource for the community regardless of the specific model.

Strong and consistent empirical gains over adapted state-of-the-art baselines (ConceptGraph, OpenFunGraph, FunGraph, KeySG) across node recall, edge recall (spatial/functional triplets), and affordance recall, with improvements holding under both GPT-4 and GPT-5 backbones for baselines, suggesting gains stem from the method rather than only backbone strength.

Thorough ablation study isolating the contribution of knowledge-guided candidate control, color-distribution features, the geometry-initialized prior graph, and multi-agent decomposition, each shown to matter for final performance.

Additional generalization checks: evaluation on the object-centric ReplicaSSG benchmark, per-dataset (non-merged) breakdown, and an efficiency comparison (GPU memory, VLM/LLM call counts) showing the method is also more computationally efficient than caption-heavy baselines.
Real-world deployment on a Stretch3 robot across four downstream tasks (QA, task planning, text query/navigation) demonstrates practical relevance beyond benchmark numbers.
Honest discussion of qualitative failure modes (part fragmentation under occlusion, reflection-induced false positives, thin-object misclassification) rather than only showcasing successes.
weaknesses: The baselines (ConceptGraph, OpenFunGraph) are not natively designed for the unified task and had to be extended by the authors with additional prompting for part/spatial/functional inference; while a reasonable necessity given no prior unified baseline exists, this raises some risk that the extensions were not optimally tuned for fairness, and the comparison should be interpreted with this caveat in mind.

The object-part knowledge base K is manually/empirically curated to 'cover common object-part relations in indoor scenes,' which partially constrains the claimed open-vocabulary generality — parts or object types not anticipated in K may still be missed, and the paper does not report how performance degrades on object categories outside the curated knowledge base.

Under strict geometric criteria (Table 4, IoU≥0.10/IoP≥0.25), part-node localization remains comparatively weak (e.g., IoU 25.8 vs. object 83.7), indicating that fine-grained part geometry is still a bottleneck despite strong semantic retrieval scores — this tempers the 'solves part grounding' framing somewhat.

Details on the human annotation protocol for UniGraph3D (number/qualification of annotators, inter-annotator agreement, time/cost) are limited, making it harder to assess annotation reliability and reproducibility of the benchmark.

The pipeline involves multiple hand-set hyperparameters (color thresholds τS, τV, fusion weights w^c, w^p, etc.); no sensitivity analysis is provided to show robustness of these choices across scenes/datasets.

Reliance on a very recent, closed-source, and likely costly LLM (GPT-5) for the reasoning stage raises reproducibility and cost concerns for practitioners wanting to replicate or deploy the system, though the paper does provide some backbone-controlled comparisons to mitigate this concern.
